items.title: “We’re not going to shoot ourselves in the foot” over Hugging Face, says OpenAI’s chief research officer
items.raw_text: Two months after the bombshell news that a swarm of its agents had broken their containment and hacked into the computers of the AI company Hugging Face , OpenAI is still putting out fires. A steady drip of disclosures about other hacks in the weeks since has kept OpenAI in the spotlight and raised serious questions about the safety of its technology. Last week brought news of another hack, this time into Australia’s national health-care system. The Australian government says that OpenAI did not notify it of the breach until 84 days after it happened. But OpenAI insists it is not on the back foot. “I do kind of reject the premise that OpenAI is a company with visible impacts in the world and therefore OpenAI is not training safe and aligned models,” says Mark Chen, the company’s chief research officer. Chen oversees OpenAI’s research teams. The recent agent hacks were accidents that happened during the testing of experimental models on his watch. In a lot of ways, the buck stops with him. I sat down with Chen in London last Friday to talk about the fallout from the hacks, what his company is doing about it, and why he thinks things are not as bad as they seem. Later that same day, OpenAI put out a report detailing yet another incident —the first since the company says it took measures to prevent them—in which its agents once again broke out onto the internet and accessed computers they were not meant to. items.title: IFLA turns 99: The countdown begins!
items.raw_text: Today IFLA celebrates its 99th birthday. Some might say that only big, round number anniversaries should be celebrated, but we haven’t made it this far by following the crowd. So, let us be defiant of expectations, and make today also an opportunity to celebrate, looking back to what we have achieved, but also looking forward to what awaits us in 2027 and well beyond. What is IFLA now, almost a century after its creation? A global community made of over 1600 members and more than 1000 active, passionate volunteers working hard to change the library field for the better. A place where we celebrate the past but look at technology, knowledge and innovation with optimism in order to achieve sustainable futures for all. An organisation that has always striven to make the world a better place. Libraries make our lives better and IFLA supports libraries globally through its international advocacy, professional standards, capacity building, and resource sharing. We have got this far because our core mission and values are lasting, giving us a key reference point and source of resilience in times of change. Today, like so many times in the past, we and the societies are being shaped and reshaped by dramatic political, economic, environmental, and social trends. items.title: Book Industry Study Group (BISG) and BookNet Canada Release 2026 Report on AI Use Across the North American Book Industry
items.raw_text: From a Joint Release: The Book Industry Study Group (BISG) and BookNet Canada have released AI Use Across the North American Book Industry 2026 , the second annual report examining how publishing professionals and organizations across the U.S. and Canada are using—and thinking about—AI. Drawing on 771 responses, this year’s report provides an opportunity to look beyond a single snapshot and begin tracking how AI adoption, attitudes, policies, and concerns are changing over time. [Clip] An Industry Moving Toward More Structured AI Use One of the clearest changes from 2025 is happening at the organizational level. In 2026, 63% of respondents said their organization is using AI, up from 48% in 2025. Individual use moved in the opposite direction, falling from 46% to 38%. Organization size also matters: 88% of organizations with more than 100 employees reported using AI. Adoption does not necessarily mean unrestricted use. The most common organizational approach is to encourage AI within controlled workflows or for specific tasks, while 49% of respondents said their organization now has an official AI policy or guidelines, up from 31% in 2025. [Clip] Concerns Remain High Greater organizational adoption has not diminished concerns about AI. Copyright remains a leading issue, cited by 86% of respondents. items.title: AI-collectiebeleid, een belangrijke rol voor de collectiespecialist
items.raw_text: AI-content krijgt een steeds grotere plek in het aanbod. Dat roept voor bibliotheken belangrijke vragen op: wat nemen we wel en niet op in de collectie, waar ligt de grens en welke rol speelt de collectiespecialist daarin? In dit blog lees je welke dilemma’s AI met zich meebrengt en waarom goede curatie en duidelijke richtlijnen steeds belangrijker worden. Donderdag 17 september kwamen 26 collectiespecialisten van 16 bibliotheken bij elkaar om het te hebben over de vraag: Wat betekent AI voor collectie en hoe gaan we ermee om? De sessie werd begeleid door DEN, kennisinstituut cultuur & digitale transformatie. Tijdens de bijeenkomst kwam duidelijk naar voren dat AI de essentie van collectie en de bibliotheek raakt. Het raakt daarbij alle aspecten van collectie, zowel het aanbod als de werkwijze. Daarnaast is duidelijk dat AI zich blijft doorontwikkelen en ook de betekenis in de maatschappij van AI nog niet helder is. Daarom gaan we jaarlijks een AI-collectiesessie organiseren waarbij we het gesprek met elkaar blijven voeren. De rol van de collectiespecialist groeit Duidelijk is dat AI-content steeds meer voorkomt en een steeds grotere plek gaat innemen in de maatschappij. Om de kwaliteit en betrouwbaarheid van de bibliotheekcollectie te waarborgen is een goede curatie cruciaal. Daarom is de rol van de collectiespecialist als curator daarbij steeds belangrijker. Most powerful obesity drug yet: People lost up to 25% of weight in trial
items.raw_text: Researchers published late-stage clinical trial data today for the latest obesity drug, retatrutide—expected to be the most powerful formula yet—and the results appear in line with high expectations. Patients with obesity on the highest retatrutide dose lost an average of 25 percent of their body weight after 80 weeks, and an average of 30 percent after an extension period to 104 weeks. Overall, more than a third of participants taking retatrutide lost 30 percent or more of their weight. The drug also proved effective at reducing knee pain (by up to 62 percent) in a subset of participants with obesity-linked knee osteoarthritis. It reduced the number of sleep apnea events per hour (by up to 57 percent) in a subset of participants with obesity-linked obstructive sleep apnea. The drug improved cardiometabolic measurements across the board, including blood pressure, triglycerides, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (bad cholesterol). At the start, more than a third of trial participants had prediabetes and, by the end, the condition had resolved in more than 90 percent of those participants. The trial began in 2023 and included 2,339 participants from 131 clinical trial sites in 11 countries. Participants were broken into four nearly equal groups, given either: 4 mg of retatrutide, 9 mg, 12 mg, or a placebo. items.title: AMD acquires World Labs AI startup, upping the ante against Nvidia
items.raw_text: Chipmaker AMD and world models company World Labs announced that AMD will acquire the AI company by the end of the year, pending regulatory approval. The transaction is valued at $8.2 billion. In 2024, computer vision scientist Fei-Fei Li founded World Labs with fellow researchers Justin Johnson, Christoph Lassner, and Ben Mildenhall, with $230 million in funding, some of which came from AMD. The company began working on new world models, which are AI models that aim to provide a useful, predictive simulation of the physical world. Competing architectures exist (earlier this year, Ars interviewed World Labs co-founder Ben Mildenhall and others in the field about exactly that), but many involve training a model on vast amounts of video data. items.title: Trump ads paid for by US government allegedly violate anti-propaganda laws
items.raw_text: Broadcasters should be ordered to stop running Trump commercials that appear to violate US laws, consumer advocacy group Public Citizen said today in a complaint to the Federal Communications Commission and Federal Trade Commission. The ads appear to violate laws against using taxpayer funds for propaganda and a law that restricts political activity by federal government employees, the group said. "The most recent of these taxpayer-funded campaign ads, entitled 'The Final Battle,' is a copied version of an ad that the Trump campaign committee issued in the 2024 election," Public Citizen wrote . "In dead serious black-and-white footage, Trump is seen marching down a corridor with a stern look, while the audio blares: 'This is the final battle. With you at my side, we will demolish the deep state. We will expel the warmongers from our government.' A notice at the bottom of the screen announces: 'Paid for by the US government.'" Trump also says in the ad, "We will cast out the communists, Marxists, and fascists. We will throw off the sick political class that hates our country, we will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate America from these villains once and for all." It uses the same video and audio from an ad Trump used in 2024 , with the main difference being that the 2024 version was paid for by Trump's campaign committee instead of the US government. The White House claims its recent ads are public service announcements. Read full article Comments

items.raw_text: For two decades, largely in service to the International Space Station, NASA has sought to foster an "economy" in low-Earth orbit. Twenty years ago, with a program to develop private spacecraft for cargo delivery to the space station, NASA sought to "stimulate efforts within the private sector to develop and operate safe, reliable, and cost-effective commercial space transportation systems." In recent years this has expanded to creating an entire commercial ecosystem in orbit, with transportation, space stations, manufacturing, tourism, and more, such that NASA is one of many customers in the market. In April 2024, the space agency explicitly laid out its philosophy: "NASA supports a robust commercial space economy that advances American industry and promotes technological discovery through in-space work and research. items.title: Here's what actually happened in OpenAI's Australian gov't server hack
items.raw_text: Last week, when Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told the world that an OpenAI agent had accessed "non-public files" from his country's Medicare statistics portal during testing, his description of the incident was a little light on details. Today, we're getting new information on just how far OpenAI's overzealous agent went in attempting to satisfy a rather innocuous-sounding informational prompt. In a newly published blog post , OpenAI says the June incident started when the company asked "an experimental, internal-only OpenAI model" to research government spending statistics in the Australian state of Victoria. When the model ran into trouble finding that data using the publicly published statistics that it was supposed to reference, "it took actions that we had not authorized it to take" to find an answer, OpenAI said. Those unauthorized actions included finding "a way to gain non-public access to the service" and using that access to view "technical system information and source code" alongside credentials and the aggregate statistics it was actually searching for, OpenAI said. This study looks at how and with whom connected cars share your data
items.raw_text: In news that should surprise very few, connected cars remain a complete privacy nightmare. But now we have a better idea of what data those cars are giving away, and to whom, thanks to a study conducted by a team of researchers at Northeastern University and Consumer Reports . Testing 21 cars from 19 different brands revealed patterns of traffic to advertisers and trackers, as well as data shared with Big Tech firms like Microsoft and Adobe. And using a car’s companion app can multiply the problem, their testing found. In 2023, the Mozilla Foundation published a widely covered report looking at the privacy policies of more than two dozen automakers. They were appalled, writing that “cars are the worst product category we have ever reviewed for privacy.” But that analysis was conducted by sitting down and reading all the various privacy policies of each brand; today’s study involved measuring traffic from actual cars under a number of scenarios, including idling and being driven. The researchers even parked 11 cars—just the electric ones—in a Faraday tent to see if the loss of a cellular signal would push that traffic to the car’s Wi-Fi connection instead. Attempts to actually see what was in the data packets using modified certificates failed in every case. items.title: Less protein for maggots means longer lives for fruit flies
items.raw_text: Back in the 1930s, scientists noticed that water fleas and rats fed restricted diets while young went on to live longer. The same effect has since turned up in fruit flies and mice. What we did not know was how a meal eaten in infancy could affect health weeks, months, or even years later. A recent Nature study might have found the answer. A team led by Fumiaki Obata, a biologist at the RIKEN Center for Biosystems Dynamics Research in Kobe, Japan, found a protein that carries a record into adulthood of what fruit flies ate as larvae, influencing how long they live. Hungry maggots Lab fruit flies are fed a mix of yeast and sugar, with yeast being their main source of protein. “We decreased only the yeast concentration in the diet, from eight percent to either one or two percent,” Obata explains. This low-protein diet was introduced roughly halfway through the larval period. Once the flies emerged from their pupae as adults, they returned to standard food. Read full article Comments

items.title: OpenAI says planned GPT-6.1 is too insecure to release
items.raw_text: OpenAI says it has canceled plans to release its updated GPT-6.1 model next month as it continues to investigate what testing shows is a safety regression compared to previous models. The move, first reported by The Wall Street Journal late Monday and later confirmed in OpenAI statements to the press, reflects what OpenAI Head of Safety Systems Saachi Jain said was a "trade off" between performance and security seen when testing the now-scrapped model. Jain said GPT-6.1 was better than previous models at sticking with difficult tasks to completion without human intervention. But the model was also more likely to fail tests related to alignment (i.e. staying within the bounds set by human creators) and more willing to use sometimes "unsafe" tools and services to push ahead with a task. It was also more likely to try to deceive end users about actions it did or didn't take, Jain said. Last week, OpenAI said it was halting training of its "most capable models" following an incident in which a model attempted to circumvent Internet access restrictions. GPT-6.1 was not among those "most capable models" covered by that move, OpenAI told the WSJ. And while GPT-6.1 won't be released as is, the company said it intends to use the same base model for further training runs that it said will hopefully lead to future GPT-6 generation models. items.title: Ouder worden? Ons taalbegrip blijft vaak verrassend sterk
items.raw_text: Het vermogen om een taal te verwerken en begrijpen blijft veel langer behouden dan vaak wordt gedacht. Nieuw onderzoek van Amerikaanse wetenschappers laat zien dat de hersengebieden die betrokken zijn bij taalbegrip opvallend goed blijven functioneren als we ouder worden. De Volkskrant schreef hierover naar aanleiding van het onderzoek dat is gepubliceerd in het wetenschappelijke tijdschrift Nature Communications. Ik vertel je er meer over. “Waar de meeste ouderen, ook als ze gezond zijn, informatie langzamer gaan verwerken en hun kortetermijngeheugen minder goed wordt, blijft hun begrip van taal op peil en kan di e zelfs verbeteren “ , blijkt uit het onderzoek. Scans laten zien dat de hersenen van ouderen taal op vrijwel dezelfde manier verwerken als die van jongere mensen. Wel plaatsen de onderzoekers een kanttekening: de studie keek alleen naar taalbegrip. Andere aspecten van taal, zoals spreken en schrijven, zijn niet onderzocht. Wat kun je hier als bibliotheek mee? Voor bibliotheken die werken aan taalontwikkeling en basisvaardigheden is dit een interessante en hoopvolle bevinding. Het onderzoek laat zien dat de hersengebieden en -netwerken die betrokken zijn bij het begrijpen van taal relatief goed behouden blijven naarmate mensen ouder worden. items.title: Actie voor nationale bundeling van academisch ai-onderzoek:
items.raw_text: Een nationaal instituut voor ai-onderzoek moet de uittocht van Nederlands ai-talent tot stilstand brengen. Als zo’n krachtenbundeling van ai-onderzoekers voldoende middelen krijgt, hoeft toptalent niet meer zijn heil te zoeken in Silicon Valley. Bovendien trekt de aanwezigheid van excellente ai-wetenschappers weer buitenlandse toppers aan. Een groep prominente Nederlandse tech-ondernemers, ondersteund door het ai-ecosysteem, is een actie begonnen voor een nationaal Ellis-instituut (European Laboratory for Learning and Intelligent Systems). Onder meer Bol.com, Booking.com, Bunq, Cradle, General Intuition, Nebius, Picnic en Techleap hebben de steunverklaring ondertekend. Nederland telt al drie Ellis-locaties, namelijk in Amsterdam, Delft en Nijmegen, met ruim 160 ai-onderzoekers. Eerder genoemde groep pleit ervoor om daarboven een nationaal instituut op te richten dat met steun van de overheid diepgaand doorbraak-onderzoek van het hoogste niveau kan doen. In Duitsland en Finland bestaat al zoiets. Zo’n nationaal centrum stelt eigen onderzoekers aan en bepaalt zijn eigen koers. Tegen de hoge salarissen en optieregelingen die Silicon Valley biedt, kan Nederland moeilijk opboksen. Maar door onderzoeksdiepte te bieden wordt het toch aantrekkelijk hier te werken. Ook gaat een nationaal lab de versnippering tegen. Nu worden de investeringen in rekenkracht en in software engineers te veel gespreid. Boven elke advertentie staat bovendien een organisch AI-antwoord dat niet te koop is, maar dat een merk wel degelijk kan beïnvloeden. Benchmarks zijn er nauwelijks, simpelweg omdat het kanaal nog te jong is om historische data te hebben opgebouwd. Precies daar zet de Emerce-training op in. items.title: ING: technologische voorloper onder Europese banken
items.raw_text: Interview | Cio Edwin Entrop Sinds 2021 is Edwin Entrop cio van ING Nederland. In die rol is hij verantwoordelijk voor de it-strategie en het verder uitbouwen van wat hij zelf de ‘bank in je broekzak’ noemt. Entrop beschouwt de ING als een technologische voorloper in de Europese bancaire wereld. De komende jaren staan in het teken van verdere digitalisering. Ai, digitale soevereiniteit en het versnellen van innovatie vormen daarbij belangrijke strategische thema’s. Met agentic development als spannende nieuwe proeftuin. Tekst – De digitale transformatie van banken is al jaren gaande, maar volgens cio Edwin Entrop komt die ontwikkeling momenteel in een stroomversnelling terecht. Kunstmatige intelligentie, geopolitieke ontwikkelingen en de groeiende afhankelijkheid van grote technologiebedrijven dwingen financiële instellingen om scherpe keuzes te maken. ING wil daarbij voorop blijven lopen. ‘Wij zien onszelf echt als een technologische voorloper en continue vernieuwer. Dat willen we ook blijven’, zegt Entrop. Hij stipt bijvoorbeeld nog even het begin dit jaar gevierde veertigjarige jubileum van Girotel van voorloper Postbank aan: de bakermat van het thuisbankieren (‘direct banking’) in Nederland. Private cloud als strategische keuze Een van de redenen waarom ING zich technologisch onderscheidt, is volgens de cio een beslissing die ruim tien jaar geleden werd genomen.
